```{=html}
<article class="paper">
  <h3 class="paper-title">The Ebb after the Wave: Explaining the Diverging Electoral Fortunes of European Green Parties after 2019</h3>
  <p class="paper-meta">Puqiu Zhao · Work in progress · 2026</p>
  <p class="paper-tags">Green Parties · Electoral Politics · Crisis</p>
  <blockquote class="paper-quote">Why did support for Green parties diverge after the 2019 green victory, and why have some parties held on to their voters in times of crisis while others have not?</blockquote>
  <div class="paper-actions">
    <a class="paper-btn" href="ebb-after-the-wave.html">Project page</a>
    <a class="paper-btn" href="ebb-after-the-wave.html#literature">Literature</a>
    <details class="paper-abstract">
      <summary>Read abstract</summary>
      <p>After the 2019 "green wave", support for Green parties across Europe moved in different directions as COVID-19 (2020) and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine (2022) hit European economies. Some Green parties lost ground; others gained it.</p>
      <p>Existing work mostly treats Green parties as one party family and explains their post-crisis decline through myopic voters who push climate concerns down the agenda when the economy deteriorates, and through issue competition with other party families. This project instead asks when voters are <em>less</em> myopic and how Green parties differ in their responses to economic downturns. The empirical analysis draws on the European Social Survey (waves 7&ndash;11, 2014&ndash;2024).</p>
    </details>
  </div>
</article>
```
